detail.longDescription: Reading List – 2026-11-24 I’m drawn to tools that let you check what will happen before you commit. A scheduling rule can read back correctly and still offer slots you didn’t mean to publish. Moving a mail domain calls for a different kind of check: keeping the old service running long enough to verify the new setup before you lose the fallback. Introducing Jacq Jacq makes it possible to experiment with GPU inference without writing every kernel from scratch in CUDA. What catches my attention about my friend Keith’s work is that you can inspect the generated CUDA and see what the compiler actually did. That matters because the model generator still uses fixed runtime templates: it parses layer and pipeline descriptions, but editing those expressions won’t change the generated computation graph. Introducing Jacq Kagi Mail is here (Public Beta) Kagi Mail’s public beta looks like a fantastic Gmail alternative to me, and what stands out is how Kagi has designed for leaving. Kagi says you can use standard clients, export your mail and calendar at any time, and keep sending and receiving for 60 days after you leave. That overlap matters when you’re moving a domain: you can verify the new setup without making cancellation and cutover the same event. Kagi Mail is here (Public Beta) How to get a morning briefing, or a wake-up call, with your calendar, email and news Pepper’s wake-up call has a delivery policy worth noticing: one ring, no voicemail, no retry. What catches my attention is that Pepper recommends adding a second destination if you rely on the brief. For anyone building scheduled notifications, I’d separate the two jobs: a chat card can preserve the briefing after a missed call, but it won’t necessarily wake anyone up. How to get a morning briefing, or a wake-up call, with your calendar, email and news How to make a booking link people can pick a time from Natural-language scheduling rules are easier to trust when you can see the slots they produce. Pepper shows both a plain-language readback and a preview that uses the same rules and calendar data as the public link. What catches my attention is the distinction between reading what the system understood and checking what it will actually offer. If you’re building a similar interface, give users both checks before they publish. The reveal transcript is mostly music with a few lines of dialogue, so it doesn’t give me much to go on beyond the announcement.
